design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: gate_proof_vocabulary_has_a_producer
title: gate proof vocabulary has a producer
pattern: A gate proves each of its axes from a fixed set of canonical measurement names, and the modules that emit measurements each carry their own name table. Nothing relates the two tables. When no emitting module carries any name an axis proves from, that axis is structurally unprovable: every run reports it as not determined, the gate's overall verdict can never be reached, and no candidate can ever be promoted. Every per-module test stays green throughout, because each module is only ever tested against its own table.
docstring: Every measurement name a gate proves from must appear in at least one emitting module's declared name table. An axis whose whole proof vocabulary is unproduced is not a strict gate; it is a gate that cannot be answered, and the flow reports it as undetermined forever while looking healthy. The check is a set difference between two tables that already exist, so it costs one pass and it covers a name added tomorrow the day it lands.
fix_action: Build the union of the emitting modules' declared name tables (the physical sign-off source list, the power category map, the area taxonomy, and a name table the timing module must gain because it composes its names with a format string today). Compare that union against the gate's per-axis proof vocabulary. Refuse, naming the axis and every name in it, when no group of an axis has a single produced name. Report the same difference in the other direction as a warning: a produced name no gate proves from is a measurement nobody reads. THE PREDICATE WAS RUN, AND IT IS BUILDABLE AS DESCRIBED. Union of the four producer registries: 8 sign-off names, 4 power names, 14 area names, and 8 timing names that had to be EXPANDED from three format strings — which is why the timing module needs a declared table before the check can read it without a parser. Against the nine axes that union gives 2 of 3, 2 of 3, 0 of 4, 1 of 1, 1 of 2, 1 of 1, 2 of 2, 2 of 2, 1 of 1 — one axis structurally unprovable, and three more carrying a proof name nothing emits, which the axis survives only because a sibling group covers it. The partial rows are the reason the report must be per proof name and not per axis. SWEPT, with the same result as its sibling and for the same reason. The table said this rule is free of false positives BY CONSTRUCTION. Verified input by input: three of the four producer registries ARE declared tables and were read directly -- 8 sign-off sources, 4 power categories, 14 area specs, 26 names total. The fourth is not a table at all: the timing module composes its metric names with THREE percent-format strings, so its 8 names exist only as the cross product of the values those two placeholders can take, and a check must expand them. An expansion that misses a value drops a name from the union, and a name missing from the union is reported as an axis with no producer -- a FALSE POSITIVE, in the direction that looks like a finding. So the construction argument covers 26 of the 34 names and not the 8 that need a parser. The remedy is already in this record and is now load-bearing rather than incidental: the timing module must gain a declared name table like the other three, after which the claim is true for all 34.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: required_scope_keys_are_emitted_by_their_producer
title: required scope keys are emitted by their producer
pattern: A comparison gate declares, per axis, the set of measurement-condition keys two numbers must both carry before they may be compared. The module that emits that axis fills the keys it happens to have. Nothing relates the two sets. A producer short of one key makes every comparison over its numbers refuse, on both arms at once, before any value is looked at — and the refusal names a key, not a producer, so it reads as a caller mistake rather than as the emitting module's gap.
docstring: Each key a comparison gate requires of an axis must be emitted by the module that produces that axis, or that module must record, beside the scope it did not fill, the reason it could not. The two-sided rule matters: a key filled with an empty or null placeholder is worse than an absent one, because two placeholders compare equal and two numbers taken under conditions nobody recorded then pass as taken under the same conditions.
fix_action: For each axis of the comparison gate's required-keys table, construct the producing module's scope on a fixture and diff the key sets. Refuse when a required key is neither emitted nor accounted for by a recorded gap reason. Refuse separately, and with a distinct code, when a required key is present with a null or empty value. THE PREDICATE WAS RUN on the power axis by building the producer's real records and diffing their scope against the consumer's table: 5 of 6 required keys satisfied, the sixth missing. That is the whole check, on one axis, in a few lines — which is the argument for it. It must be driven per axis over the whole required table rather than per producer, because a producer emits scope for more than one axis and satisfying one says nothing about the next. THE RULE ALREADY HAS A WORKING REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION IN A SIBLING MODULE OF THE SAME LAYER, and the implementing lane should copy it rather than invent one. The timing producer declares a fixed key set that is ALWAYS PRESENT — 7 of the 7 its axis requires — and its suite refuses both a missing key and an UNDECLARED EXTRA, on the stated ground that a key nobody declared makes a record incomparable to every other record. The two producers between them evidence both clauses of this rule: one is short a key, and the other has been seen writing a key that is present and null, which the comparison refuses under a different code precisely because two nulls compare equal. Absent, present-and-null, and undeclared-extra are three distinct verdicts and the check owes all three. SWEPT, and the sweep contradicts the reason this rule was left unswept. The table said it is free of false positives BY CONSTRUCTION, because a set difference cannot invent a member. That holds only if BOTH sides are declared, and only one is. The required side is a real declared table keyed by axis. The emitted side is declared for exactly ONE of the three axes it covers -- the timing module names its scope keys in a module-level tuple; the power module declares a single key and assembles the rest inline; the area module declares none at all. So for two of three axes the check must DERIVE what the producer emits, and a derived set can be wrong in the direction that manufactures a false positive, which is the failure this lane has recorded seventeen times. BUILD IT SO THE CLAIM BECOMES TRUE: require each producer to declare the scope key set it emits, in the shape the timing module already uses, and make the check a difference over two declared tables. Then FP-freedom is a property of the design rather than an assertion about it, and the rule covers 3 of 3 axes instead of 1.

design: plugin test suite, layer-wide; no design involved
rule_name: population_guard_asserts_equality_not_a_floor
title: population guard asserts equality not a floor
pattern: A suite parametrises over a population it DISCOVERS (a glob, a package walk) but drives each member with an invocation it DECLARES (a hand-maintained table or a literal tuple). The guard against an empty population is written as a floor — at least N — with N frozen at the count on the day the two numbers happened to agree. The floor then passes forever while the two sets drift apart, so a member added later is silently uncovered, and an entry left behind for a member since deleted is invisible in the other direction. The class is not confined to test files and it is not confined to invocation tables: any place a literal list stands in for a population the code could enumerate has it, INCLUDING inside a census written to fix this very defect, which is where it is hardest to see because the file's subject is the rule it breaks.
docstring: A population guard over a discovered set must assert EQUALITY against the declared set and print the symmetric difference, never a lower bound. A lower bound answers a question nobody asked — is the population non-empty — while the question that matters is whether every discovered member is declared and every declared member still exists. A floor cannot see either drift, and it reads as coverage while holding neither.
fix_action: Replace the floor assertion with a set-equality assertion between the discovered population and the declared table, whose message prints both counts and both directions of the difference. Emit it ONCE for the whole population rather than once per member, so the reader gets the list instead of N single names. THE OBVIOUS WRONG GUARD, and one is already in the tree: asserting the declared table against ITS OWN length. That is self-consistency; it passes for any table and can never see the population. Assert against the POPULATION. Where several declared tables cover one discovered population, assert each against it and assert the tables agree with one another — the defect is not confined to invocation tables: the same shape sits on the present-but-empty input table and on the hand-listed producer set, whose discovered counterpart is an importable package. NOTE ON WHERE THIS LIVES: no program in this tree audits a test suite's own population arithmetic, so this routes to the gate that stands between a plugin change and a completion claim. Its natural home is a new member of the meta-gate family that already audits the program population for wiring and for a disclosed denominator; build it there and this gate calls it. COUNT THE OTHER SITES BEFORE BUILDING: measured on this tree the same shape sits on SIX tables of one layer — two invocation tables at 15 of 19, a present-but-empty input table at 8 of 19, a hand-named producer trio, a literal backend tuple whose package is importable, and the envelope-producer direction of the census at three literals. Only the first was known when this record was written; the other five came from asking the question once per table. A fix that repairs one table and leaves five is the floor again at a different altitude. CORPUS-SWEPT: the suite holds 161 floor assertions of this shape, of which 36 are over a population the file DISCOVERS and carry a bound above one — that is the rule's population and it is tractable. The discriminator is the bound: `>= 1` is a non-emptiness check, a different and legitimate assertion, and flagging it would bury the 36 under the 125. The four tables this record was written from are among the 36. THE HARM IS MEASURED, NOT HYPOTHETICAL, AND THE DECLARED TABLE IS WHAT PREVENTS IT. All 15 declared invocations correctly name a required argument of their own program — so where the table reaches, an invented arm is impossible. The one false reading on record happened on a program OUTSIDE it: an investigator handed an empty directory to a command whose actual input is a document, read the resulting pass as a vacuous one, and was wrong. That is what an uncovered member costs — not merely absent coverage, but a confident wrong answer produced by whoever fills the gap by guessing. And the harm compounds: a command outside the declared population was measured answering a settled question the wrong way, while the lane that found it could not tell the question was settled — the assertion that settles it walks the same population the command is missing from. A SEVENTH INSTANCE, and it is not a test table this time — the same shape in a RUNNER. A basis stamp that a consumer stages from is written at 16 sites in one emitter, and no test enumerates them: each test names the one report it cares about. So a seventeenth emitter added tomorrow stamps nothing and every existing test stays green, which is exactly how the defect that started this cluster reached a published run. The population is the emitters, it is enumerable from the source, and nothing enumerates it. AN EIGHTH INSTANCE, and this one is a gate that LANDED during this branch: `programs/generated_test_list_min_guard.py` checks a generated test list against a MINIMUM and a resolvable path set instead of against emptiness. That is a real improvement on 'not empty' and it is exactly the floor this record says is not enough -- a minimum cannot see a list that should hold 40 and holds 39. The two compose: keep its resolvable-path arm, and replace the floor with the declared-versus-discovered equality this record specifies. Whoever builds this should start from that file, not from scratch. A SIBLING SHAPE -- a guard defeated by a production default rather than by a miscounted population -- is recorded separately as its own rule, because folding a distinct failure into this record is how the two gaps this lane already caught came to be hidden.

design: plugin test suite, layer-wide; no design involved
rule_name: layer_membership_is_declared_not_inferred_from_a_filename_prefix
title: layer membership is declared not inferred from a filename prefix
pattern: A suite that enforces a LAYER-wide property selects its population with a filename-prefix glob, because in the layer's first week the prefix and the layer were the same set. They stop being the same set as soon as the layer gains a module inside its own package, or a program that imports the layer under a different name. Every such executable is outside the population, so the layer property is unenforced on it — and the defect the suite exists to catch survives there untouched, with the suite green.
docstring: Membership of a layer is a RELATION — the executable imports the layer's package, or cites the layer's interface document — and it must be computed from that relation, never from how the file happens to be named. A naming convention standing in for a boundary silently shrinks the population every time the layer grows in a direction the convention did not anticipate, and the shrinkage is invisible because the members that fell out were never counted.
fix_action: Define the population as every executable that imports the layer's package or cites the layer's interface document, and take the prefix glob as one contributor rather than as the definition. Assert that the relation-derived population is a superset of the glob-derived one, and drive every arm of the layer property over the relation-derived set. NOTE ON WHERE THIS LIVES: same home as the population-equality rule, and they share a helper — the relation-derived population is the input both need, so computing it twice is how the two answers start to disagree. CORPUS-SWEPT, AND IT NEEDS A DISCRIMINATOR THE RECORD DID NOT HAVE: 32 test files select a population by filename prefix, and MOST ARE CORRECT — the universal prefix that means `every test` is exactly the right selector for a suite-wide property. The rule fires only where the prefix stands in for a SEMANTIC SUBSET, a layer or a family, because that is where the naming convention and the boundary can drift apart. Distinguish them by whether the prefix names a subset at all: the universal one has no sibling population it could be missing. AND THE COST OF BEING OUTSIDE THE POPULATION IS A WRONG ANSWER, NOT A MISSING ONE. The one false vacuous reading on record was taken against a program the prefix does not reach: its input is a document and it was handed an empty directory, so it answered correctly about a population nobody had asked it about. Members outside the boundary do not sit un-examined; they get examined by improvised arms, which is worse. A THIRD MEASURED INSTANCE, AND IT RESOLVES A QUESTION A LANE LEFT OPEN. Two commands of one layer answer the same question — a readable input that yields nothing — with different codes: one returns 0 and the other returns 2. A lane reported the disagreement and said it could not establish from the code which was the layer's answer. The layer HAS an answer: its own present-but-empty test asserts 2, three times. The reason nobody could see it is that the answer lives in a test whose population is the prefix, and the command returning 0 is one of the executables the prefix misses. So the boundary does not merely leave members unchecked; it hides the settled answer from the people who own them. RE-MEASURED after merging 30 commits of main: the six rc codes are unchanged (2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3) and a flag that exists still returns 0, so the finding is current rather than carried forward. The two offenders now have a named home: main landed `programs/_gate_usage_exit.py`, which exists because rc 2 already means VACUOUS and a bad invocation therefore needs rc 3. The 'one-line shared fix' this record asks for is that module, so the implementing lane imports it rather than writing the constant again.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: two_input_selectors_given_together_must_refuse
title: two input selectors given together must refuse
pattern: A tool grows a second way to name its input — a directory of many alongside the single positional one — and the two are wired as independent options rather than as alternatives. Given both, the later branch wins and the other input is never opened. Nothing is printed about the input that was dropped, so a caller who names a failing record and adds the directory flag is told the directory's verdict and never learns the record was not read. The exit code changes with it, from a finding to a could-not-check, which reads as an improvement.
docstring: Two selectors that name the same input in different ways are ALTERNATIVES and must be declared as such: given both, refuse as a bad invocation and name both. Silently letting one shadow the other converts a real verdict into a different verdict on an unrelated population, and the caller has no way to tell — the output is well-formed and describes work that was genuinely done, just not on the thing they named.
fix_action: Put the single-target and the collection selectors in one mutually exclusive group so the argument parser itself refuses both, and return the bad-invocation exit code rather than the could-not-check one. Where an existing caller depends on passing both, adjudicate BOTH populations and aggregate under the most-severe rule; never pick one silently. Add the both-given case to the layer's bad-invocation arm so every tool in the layer is covered by the same test rather than this one. CORPUS-SWEPT, BY EXECUTION. The earlier sweep for this record screened SOURCE for an argparse mutual-exclusion group and reported that not one of nine commands declared one. That screen was true and misleading: this layer's own remedy is not an argparse group at all but a shared seam, `both_given` in the module `_ppa_corpus`, which four gates call and which a per-file grep for the exit constant cannot see because the constant lives in the seam. The population was therefore re-measured by RUNNING each command with both selectors and reading the exit code. Eight commands take both a single target and a real collection selector. Four gates outside that eight refuse correctly through the seam with the bad-invocation code, naming both selectors and saying why -- that is the remedy shape to copy, and it beats an argparse group because the parser's own message names neither the conflict nor the consequence. Of the eight: six silently pick one and return a verdict about the input the caller did not name; one, the step-internal bubble-up gate, prints a correct refusal that names both and calls them mutually exclusive but returns the NOT-CHECKED code instead of the bad-invocation one, so a caller screening exit codes cannot distinguish it from a gate that merely found no artefacts; and one, the phase-one quality gate, returns a GREEN PASS on `Scanned 0 ICs`, which is the worst of the three because both other outcomes at least decline to claim success. So the rule has three distinct failure shapes to detect, not one, and an implementation that only adds a mutual-exclusion group would fix six of the eight and leave the wrong-code and vacuous-pass cases exactly as they are.

design: shipped plugin tree, any host; no design involved
rule_name: runtime_output_path_may_not_resolve_inside_the_installed_tree
title: a runtime output path may not resolve inside the installed tree
pattern: A tool takes an output path from the caller and writes it as given. A relative path is resolved against the process working directory, which for a tool invoked from inside the installation is the installation. The write then creates directories and files inside the INSTALLED product, where they survive the run, appear as untracked additions, and can be picked up by the next hygiene or packaging pass as if they were shipped content. The failure is invisible to the caller because the write succeeds.
docstring: An artefact written on behalf of a caller belongs to that caller's run, so its resolved destination must lie outside the installed product tree. Resolve the destination before opening it and refuse when it falls inside the installation, naming both the resolved path and the installation root. The refusal must happen BEFORE any directory is created: a run that refuses and still leaves a directory behind has done the damage it declined to do, which is worse than either outcome alone.
fix_action: In the shared atomic writer, resolve the destination and compare it against the installation root computed from the module's own location. Refuse with the bad-invocation code before creating any parent directory. Two properties must be tested rather than assumed: that the refusal fires on a relative path when the working directory is the installation, and that after a refusal the tree carries no new entry — the measured case refused with the could-not-check code AND still wrote the file and its parent directory. NEAREST PRIOR ART, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT REACH: a shipped guard already blocks a TEST RUN that leaves the tree it tests dirty, and it exists because three writers into the installed tree were each found by accident. It is scoped to a suite session and it looks AFTER the fact, at the working tree's status. A person running a shipped command outside any session is not in its population, and the write has already happened when it would look. Do not rebuild it and do not treat it as coverage: the new rule refuses at the write site, before the directory is created, on every invocation. CORPUS-SWEPT, AND THE RESULT IS ABOUT PLACEMENT: zero programs in the shared writer's population write to a destination literal inside the installed tree, so the guard has NO false positives where the record puts it. The tree's two real in-tree regenerators live outside that population, at repository root, and neither imports the shared writer. That is a placement warning, not an all-clear: the same predicate hung on a broader hook — anything that refuses writes into the tree generally — WOULD catch them, and they are legitimate. Put it in the shared writer, and if the regenerators ever adopt that writer they need a declared exemption. THE REPRODUCTION, EXACTLY: invoke a record-producing command from inside the installation with a relative output path. It exits 2 — an honest refusal — and it has ALREADY created the parent directory and written the file, which the version-control status then reports as a new untracked entry in the shipped product. Both halves matter: the exit code is right and the side effect happened anyway, so a caller who checks only the code sees correct behaviour and a tree that has been modified. A STRONGER REPRODUCTION, FOUND BY ACCIDENT WHILE PROBING SOMETHING ELSE: the caller need not supply anything. One command carries a RELATIVE DEFAULT output path, so invoking it from inside the installation with NO ARGUMENTS AT ALL creates a directory and writes a file into the shipped product — and returns SUCCESS while doing it. That is worse than the refused-but-wrote case in two ways: there is no caller mistake to blame, and there is no non-zero exit code to notice. It is also the case an ordinary user hits first, because running a tool with no arguments to see what it does is what people do. The check must therefore cover DEFAULTS, not only caller-supplied paths: resolve the destination after defaulting and before opening it. SWEPT, and the sweep settles WHERE the check goes, which the record had argued for on reasoning alone. Across the program tree: 1238 programs, 759 declaring an output-path option, and 7 carrying a RELATIVE default. A static scan for that shape is the obvious implementation and it is the wrong one -- several of the 7 are correct. A template generator whose default writes a template file beside the caller, and an audit whose default writes under a conventional reports directory, are both right when the caller is standing in a project, and both wrong only when the caller is standing inside the installed product. The offending property is therefore not the relative default but WHERE IT RESOLVES AT RUNTIME, which a static screen cannot see: it would report 7 findings of which only the ones invoked from inside the install are real, and the count would change with nothing but the caller's directory. So the check belongs at the write site in the shared writer, resolving the path and comparing it against the installation root before creating anything -- which is what this record already specified, now with the measurement that rules out the cheaper alternative.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: published_absence_claim_is_rechecked_against_the_tree
title: a published absence claim is rechecked against the tree
pattern: A placeholder implementation carries an explanatory string saying WHY it cannot answer, and that string names a module or artefact as not yet present. The named thing lands later, in a different change, and the string is never revisited — it is a literal in a file nobody had reason to reopen. The stale claim is then copied verbatim into every document the placeholder publishes, where it reads as a current statement about the tree and is believed, because a provenance note is exactly the field a reader does not audit.
docstring: A published explanation that asserts a named artefact is ABSENT must be re-evaluated against the tree at the moment it is published, not written as a literal. Two qualifications decide the whole rule and both are structural. The absence verb must attach to THAT path — sharing a docstring with it is not attachment. And the claim must be UNCONDITIONAL: a message emitted only on the branch where the artefact was found missing is correct by construction and must never be flagged. What is refused is a claim that is published whatever the tree says, which is the only form that can go stale silently.
fix_action: Walk the string literals of the program layer. For each absence verb, take only paths within a short window of it, so the verb attaches to the path rather than merely sharing a docstring. Resolve each path; keep the ones that EXIST. Then discard every remaining hit whose literal is reachable only through a branch whose test mentions that artefact — those are correct messages on the not-found path. Refuse what is left: a claim of absence that is published unconditionally about something present. CORPUS-SWEPT ON THIS TREE, AND THE SWEEP IS WHERE BOTH QUALIFICATIONS CAME FROM. Matching a verb and a path anywhere in one literal gives 560 hits over 119,359 literals, all of them a module docstring naming a file in one paragraph and using an absence phrase in another. Requiring proximity gives 85 at a wide window, 14 at a medium one and 6 at a tight one. Reading those 6: four attach the verb to a different noun in the same sentence, and two are messages on a not-found branch. ZERO real defects remain, so this rule runs CLEAN on the tree today — the instance that motivated it has since been fixed at its one site. It is the only rule in this set that meets the run-clean bar outright, and it is worth having anyway: the fixed site was guarded by hand for one string, and nothing stops the next stub from carrying the next one.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: metric_constant_across_differing_arms_is_not_measured
title: a metric constant across arms that differ is not measured under that lever
pattern: A sweep turns a lever and records an objective on each arm. One axis of the objective is computed by a session whose inputs the lever cannot reach — it reads an upstream intermediate rather than the artefact the lever rewrote. The axis then returns the SAME value on every arm while every arm's actual artefacts differ. No individual number looks wrong, no gate fires, and the sweep publishes the axis as searched. A reader concludes the lever does not affect that axis, which is the exact opposite of what happened.
docstring: Across a set of arms whose implementations provably differ, an axis taking ONE distinct value on every arm is a candidate for not having been measured downstream of the lever. It is only a CANDIDATE: a clean design is clean on every arm, so a zero-valued count that is invariant is usually correct and flagging it is noise. The discriminator is a SIBLING measuring the same quantity from the same artefact: when one reading of a quantity moves across the arms and another reading of that same quantity does not, the frozen one is not describing the arms. That test needs no reference measurement and no knowledge of what the right value would be, which is what lets it run inside the flow.
fix_action: At sweep publication, for each axis over the arms that RAN: count distinct values and distinct implementation identities. Group axes into families sharing their leading name segments. Report an axis when the arms carry two or more implementation identities, the axis carries exactly one value, AND some sibling in its family carries more than one. Name the axis, the frozen value, the sibling and its spread. Raise the severity when the frozen value is a numeric sentinel, because a sentinel is what an un-analysed report prints. Two arms make it non-vacuous, so do not gate it behind a minimum sweep size; a one-arm sweep is skipped and SAYS it was skipped. CORPUS-SWEPT ON A REAL 21-ARM PUBLISHED SWEEP, AND NARROWED BY IT: the invariance test alone flags 24 of 54 axes, which is unusable — most are a clean design being clean on every arm. Adding the varying-sibling condition gives 8; requiring the frozen value to be a sentinel as well gives 4. Ship the two-condition form and report the sentinel as severity, not as a filter, because a legitimately-zero count with a varying sibling is a real pattern too. THE TOP HIT IS A LIVE DEFECT AND IT WAS FOUND INDEPENDENTLY BY ANOTHER ROUTE: a timing summary frozen at the sentinel on all 21 arms while its sibling reading of the same quantity spreads over 20 distinct values, from a multi-corner report whose corner key the comparison gate separately refuses as null. Two methods with nothing in common converging on one record is the strongest evidence either can give, and this method adds what the other cannot: the number itself does not move when the thing it measures does.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
title: A generated report header must be derived from the inputs the session actually opened
why_not_bucket_a: A program can decide this and the predicate is trivial — compare the claim against the input list — but no emitter records the inputs it opened, so today the check has nothing to read. The work is the provenance plumbing across every emitter, not the predicate, which is why this is a backlog item rather than a rule someone can add to one file.
pattern: A generated document describes its own basis in a header written as prose literals, while the session that produced it takes its inputs from variables resolved at run time. The two drift the first time a caller reaches the emitter by a path the header's author did not have in mind, and the document then states a basis the session never had. Nothing downstream can detect it: the header is well-formed, the numbers are real numbers produced by the real tool, and the only witness is the input list, which the document does not carry.
suggested_fix: Give every emitter a recorded list of the inputs it opened, and derive every self-describing line of the header from that list rather than from a literal. Then a single gate can assert, for any generated document, that each basis claim in its header is entailed by its own input list — and an emitter that claims a basis it cannot support fails at emission rather than at review. The degradation rule comes with it: when the intended input is missing, the emitter falls back AND the header, the stamp and the provenance envelope all name what was actually linked. MEASURED on the instance that motivated it: the shipped figure was 1.873x low and one whole group of the breakdown read exactly 0.000, because the session linked an input from before the stage the header claimed. The stronger evidence needs no reference at all — across a 60-configuration sweep the report was byte-identical 60 times while all 60 of the inputs it claimed to describe differed.
session_context: Raised while distilling an end-to-end drive of the measurement layer over one routed core. The instance that produced it has since been fixed in its own emitter by exactly this technique, which is what makes the general form worth building: the technique is known to work and is applied in one place out of many.

design: twelve arms of a seventy-arm cross-layer sweep, open PDK
problem: OpenROAD is killed by signal 11 during post-route design-rule repair, AFTER detailed routing has printed its own completion line, on every arm whose accumulator is non-redundant. Ten of ten such arms crash; none of the fifty-two arms that preserve the state encoding crash. The process exit is 139, the route itself completed, and the crash is therefore in the post-route repair stage rather than in routing.
golden_sample: ppa-crosslayer/records/trials/c02/ — a state-encoding-preserving arm of the same sweep, same tool build, same PDK, same script, which completes the post-route tail normally
bad_sample: ppa-crosslayer/records/trials/x03/ and x04, x11, x12, x13, y03, y04, y08, z24, z25 — ten reproductions of the same crash. EVIDENCE GAP, measured while re-reading this record and stated here because a fork maintainer will hit it first: the ten directories are committed and tracked, but each holds only objective.json, records.json and run.json. None carries a log, a report or an error file, and each records runner_rc 1 -- not the 139 this record cites. The golden records runner_rc 1 as well, so the committed artefacts do not distinguish the crashing arms from the passing one on the only status field they carry. The signal, the exit code and the router's completion line come from the originating lane's session output, which was never committed. This is exactly the defect A-15 records -- the producing step retained nothing from the tool -- appearing in this batch's own Bucket-T evidence. The correlation that IS supported by the tree stands: 10 of 10 arms with a non-redundant accumulator fail and 0 of 52 preserving arms do, which is a netlist property and is the lead. Before this is filed upstream it needs the crash artefacts attached: the tool's stderr tail, its exit status as the tool reported it, and the post-route netlist for one crashing arm
tool_enhancement: Post-route design-rule repair must not fault on the netlist shape these arms produce; a repair pass that cannot proceed on a given instance is required to report that instance and continue or exit with a diagnostic, never to fault. The correlation is the lead: every crashing arm carries a non-redundant accumulator and no preserving arm crashes, so the reproduction is a netlist property rather than a floorplan or a random seed. Two properties the fix must hold: the ten samples above complete the post-route tail, and the tool exits non-zero with a named diagnostic rather than a signal on any instance it still cannot repair. FILING PRECONDITION: this cannot be filed as-is. The bad samples do not contain the crash, so a maintainer receiving them can reproduce nothing. Attach the tool's own exit status and stderr tail for at least one arm first; A-15 is the rule that stops the next Bucket-T record from being assembled this way. AND THE WINDOW HAS CLOSED, checked rather than assumed: the two run trees the provenance paths point at are both gone from this host, so the tool's exit status and output tail cannot be recovered by looking -- only by RE-RUNNING one crashing arm. Whoever files this should budget that run rather than go searching.
why_not_bucket_a: The fault is inside the forked tool's post-route repair stage; the flow's own classification and resume path already behave correctly — they name the crash, distinguish it from a routing failure, and re-run the tail with the faulting pass omitted. Any further plugin-side rule could only widen that workaround, and on two arms the resume already consumed the whole trial budget.
title: Post-route design-rule repair faults on a netlist shape after routing completes
pattern: A tool stage that runs AFTER the stage whose success it depends on faults rather than diagnosing, so the flow sees a signal instead of a message. The flow can classify it and route around it, but every arm carrying the triggering netlist property pays the cost of the workaround, and on the slowest arms the workaround consumes the budget the arm needed to produce a number at all.
suggested_fix: See the tool enhancement field: the faulting stage must degrade to a named diagnostic. The correlated netlist property in the samples is the reproduction path.
session_context: Ten of ten reproductions in one seventy-arm cross-layer sweep, all in the same design family, none in the fifty-two arms of the other family. Samples are committed in the sweep's own record tree.

design: the capture tooling itself; no design involved
rule_name: writer_enforces_the_field_shapes_its_consumer_requires
title: a writer enforces the field shapes its declared consumer requires
pattern: One tool WRITES a document and a second tool VALIDATES it. The writer's own schema documents a field as free text; the validator requires that field to match a fixed prefixed form. Each side is self-consistent and each side's tests pass. The writer accepts and emits the malformed document with no complaint, so the refusal arrives later, from a different tool, in a different run, and only if somebody thinks to run it — by which time the document has been filed and the author has moved on.
docstring: A writer that produces a document for a declared validator must apply that validator's field-shape rules AT WRITE TIME, not leave them to be discovered downstream. The two rule sets must come from one place: a shape restated in a second file is a shape that will disagree with the first. Measured cost of the split: the writer's own documentation gave no hint the field was constrained at all, so the natural reading produced a document its sibling refused.
fix_action: Import the validator's field-shape rules into the writer and apply them to every field the validator constrains, before the file is written; refuse with the validator's own message so the two tools cannot disagree about what is wrong. State the constrained shape in the writer's schema documentation as well, since an author reads the writer's contract and never the validator's. Add a two-directional test: a well-shaped field writes and validates, and a free-text field is refused BY THE WRITER rather than only by the validator. MEASURED: 6 of the 29 backlog records already filed in this tree fail the shape rule their own validator enforces, and both records this lane emitted were refused on first write — by an author reading the writer's contract, which documents the field as free text. RE-MEASURED after merging main, and the number moved the wrong way: 6 of 29 in-tree backlogs became 10 of 33. Every one of the four new failures came from the three SIBLING capture lanes that landed the same night, running this same loop with this same emitter -- their component values are free-text phrases like a stage description or a single word, and the validator refuses all of them. This lane's own backlogs pass, and only because the refusal is what produced this record: I hit it on my first two and changed the values. That is the whole argument for the rule in one measurement -- three authors who did not happen to run the sibling validator shipped artefacts it rejects, and nothing in the emit path told them. The population is every field the validator constrains, the predicate is the validator's own compiled shapes imported rather than restated, and the refusal is at emit time where the author is still present.

design: the capture tooling itself; no design involved
rule_name: accepted_value_branch_can_express_its_own_vocabulary
title: an accepted-value branch must be able to express its own vocabulary
pattern: A validator accepts a prefixed value and names, per prefix, the vocabulary the suffix is drawn from. One branch's suffix pattern cannot express any member of the vocabulary it names — every member carries a character the pattern excludes. The branch is therefore dead: it matches nothing, it has never matched anything, and it never will. Nothing detects this, because a branch that refuses everything looks exactly like a branch nobody has used yet, and the error message lists it among the supported forms.
docstring: Where a validator's accepted form names a vocabulary that exists in the tree, at least one member of that vocabulary must satisfy the form; a branch satisfied by no member is dead and must fail the suite rather than sit in the help text. The check is the vocabulary itself run through the pattern — a single pass over a list that is already machine-readable — so it stays true as either side changes, which is the only way it catches the case where the vocabulary gains its separator later.
fix_action: For every branch of an accepted-value pattern that names an enumerable in-tree vocabulary, run every member of that vocabulary through the branch and assert at least one is accepted. Report the branch, the vocabulary size, and the accepted count. Measured on this tree: the branch naming the flow's canonical steps accepts 0 of 42 of them, because every canonical step identifier is dotted and the branch's suffix admits only word characters and hyphens. Widen the suffix to the vocabulary's real character set, and add the census so the next divergence fails at the suite rather than at a filing. THIRD INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION, UNPROMPTED: while filing a record in this very batch I reached for the branch again — the natural component for a host-independence item is the flow step that owns it — and was refused a third time. An author who knows the branch is dead still reaches for it, because it is the correct-looking answer and the error message lists it among the supported forms. A dead branch is not merely unused; it actively costs every author who trusts the help text. CORPUS-SWEPT, AND THE POPULATION IS ONE. Exactly one prefixed-value pattern of this shape exists in the layer — the one this record is about. The defect is live and thrice-confirmed, so it is worth fixing; but as a GUARD this rule protects a population of one, and that is the honest measure of its value. It is cheap enough to be worth having anyway, because the cost of the next one is another author refused by a branch the help text advertises. AND HERE IS WHERE IT LANDS, found by reading the emitted backlog as the triager who receives it rather than as the author who wrote it. The Bucket-T ticket in this very bundle declares `root_cause_layer: forked_tool` and names its tool, and its `component` field -- the one a tracker routes on -- said `program:` followed by a plugin runner. A forked-tool bug addressed to a plugin maintainer. The cause is this record: the branch that should have carried it cannot express a dotted step identifier, so the author falls back to a prefix that is wrong. WORSE, and this is the sharper half: `fork:` and `tool:` are BOTH refused, so the accepted-value set has no term for a layer the record schema itself declares. Two fields of one record disagree about what kinds of thing exist. The ticket now says `flow:phase3`, which is expressible and merely coarse rather than false, and that is the best the grammar allows. So the check must run in both directions: every value the routing vocabulary admits must be reachable, AND every layer the schema declares must have a value that names it. SWEPT, and the result is a BOUNDARY rather than a finding, which is the more useful outcome for whoever builds this. The obvious move is to widen the rule from one prefix grammar to every accepted-value set in the tree. Measured: the tree holds 29 argparse choice sets with two or more alternatives, and the grammar-shaped form -- a prefix alternation whose suffix must then express a vocabulary -- has a population of exactly ONE, the instance this record is about. Applied to the 29, the rule finds nothing: 0 offered values are unhandled. It took three passes to establish that, and each reduction removed my own false positives -- 10, then 2, then 0. The first counted a literal appearing once in its own file as dead, which flags every value passed through to a callee; the second failed to extract the destination of a POSITIONAL argument and flagged both of its choices. DO NOT widen this rule to accepted-value sets in general: for a plain choice list, whether an offered value is handled is not statically decidable once the value is passed onward, and a screen that tries reports findings that dissolve on reading. The rule holds where a branch names a vocabulary AND constrains its shape, because only there can the constraint contradict the vocabulary.

design: two committed record trees of one measurement layer; open PDK
rule_name: discovery_selects_on_the_parsed_document_not_the_filename
title: discovery selects on the parsed document not on the filename
pattern: A gate finds its inputs with a filename glob carrying a semantic token. The complaint the glob was written to answer is that a conforming record filed under another name goes unjudged — and a filename glob answers that complaint with a smaller version of itself. It fails in both directions at once: a conforming document whose name lacks the token is never read, and a NON-input whose name carries the token is read as an input, which for a gate that names its own output report after itself means the gate adjudicates its own verdict. The disclosed denominator does not save it, because the denominator is counted over the already-name-filtered population.
docstring: Discovery of typed input must select on the PARSED DOCUMENT — its declared schema, or where none is declared a structural predicate stated in the code — and never on the file's name. A name is a convention the producer may not have been told about, and it is chosen by the same author whose mistake the gate exists to catch. The output-document case must be excluded explicitly rather than by hoping its name differs: a gate that reads its own verdict as an input reports the pass it already wrote.
fix_action: Walk every candidate file under the root, parse it, and select on the declared schema identifier; where a document class declares none, select on a structural predicate and state that predicate in the code beside the selector. Exclude the gate's own output schemas by name of SCHEMA, not by name of file, and add a test that builds a real report with the real command, drops it in the corpus and asserts the vacuous refusal. Disclose three numbers on every run, not one: files opened, records selected, and files that could not be parsed — a file nobody could read is not a file that held no record, and it must raise the verdict rather than shrink the denominator quietly. Measured on the two committed record trees of this layer: 582 documents of which 15 declare the comparison schema, name-glob selects 0; and 496 documents of which 2 declare it, name-glob selects 4 — two records and two of the gate's own reports. A SECOND INSTANCE, IN THE SAME LAYER AND SHARPER: the timing module selects sign-off reports by a name pattern under three named directories, and its own comment claims that a new corner report is therefore picked up without a change to the module. Measured against the report names the flow's own runner writes, the pattern reaches 8 of 13 timing-shaped reports — and one of the five it misses is a report the SAME runner deliberately stamps with the basis marker this module reads. Some of the five may be out of scope on purpose; nothing in the selector says which, and that is the defect rather than the count. A structural selector states the intent it is currently leaving to a prefix. CORPUS-SWEPT, AND THE POPULATION IS NOT WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. Applied to every filename pattern in the program layer the rule flags 362 of 1584, and the overwhelming majority are correct: a layer reading artefacts it wrote itself, under names it chose, in a directory it owns. There is no two-author problem there and flagging it is noise. The population where the rule holds is a scan over a CALLER-SUPPLIED corpus, whose documents may have been written by a producer this layer never saw — measured here as 12 programs, not 362 sites, which makes the check per-scanner and tractable. Scope it that way. AND FOLLOW CONSTANTS: a screen that reads only the literal argument of the discovery call finds 4 of the 12 and MISSES THE CASE THAT MOTIVATED THIS RULE, whose pattern is a module-level constant. That is the third time in this batch a naive screen has failed on the very case it was written for. SPLIT OFF THE SECOND INSTANCE: the timing-report case is a different rule wearing the same clothes. It is same-layer, so the corpus argument does not apply; what is wrong there is that the module's own comment CLAIMS a new report is picked up without a change and the pattern does not deliver that. That belongs with the documented-claim family, not here. ITS MOTIVATING INSTANCE WAS FIXED ON MAIN DURING THIS LANE, and the record is NOT withdrawn -- which is the distinction the brief asks for and the reason it asks. The comparison gate no longer guesses at filenames: the glob is gone from the tree, the program now reads a declared schema field, and a landed test states the old defect in the same terms this record does, including the corpus that reported 0 records while 15 declared ones sat in it. That is one site. The SECOND instance, in the same layer, is untouched: the timing module still selects sign-off reports by a filename prefix, the constant is unchanged, and its own comment still promises that a new corner report is picked up without a change there -- which was measured false, 8 of 13 reached. So the class survives its own most visible instance being repaired, in a module nobody had reason to touch, which is exactly the case the brief names: a fix that landed is where the distilled rule is missing, because the next occurrence is somewhere the fix did not look.

design: any host carrying an older release of an optional dependency; no design involved
title: An optional dependency needs a version matrix, because present-but-too-old is the arm nothing tests
why_not_bucket_a: A program cannot decide this from the source: I built the static check four ways and every one over-reported, and all six survivors I could execute degraded correctly. The input that would settle it — the dependency INSTALLED AT AN OLDER RELEASE — does not exist on the host at check time, and no amount of reading the code conjures it. Producing that input is a version matrix in CI, and that is the engineering.
pattern: An optional dependency is handled for the case where it is ABSENT — the import is guarded, the fallback degrades, and that path is usually correct because it is the case the author imagined. The case that bites is PRESENT BUT TOO OLD: the import succeeds, the guard never runs, and an attribute added in a later release raises inside a program whose exit codes reserve a value for a finding about the subject under test. So a crash publishes itself as a verdict. Absent and too-old are different states and only the first is an import failure; every test that skips on importability covers the first and reports the second as an unexplained red.
suggested_fix: Add a CI arm that installs each optional dependency at the oldest release the plugin claims to support, and run the suite there. That arm is the only thing that can distinguish the two states, and it is what turns a red on somebody's machine into a red on ours. Alongside it, the cheap half is worth having: where a guarded import is followed by an attribute the fallback cannot supply, the fallback should set an explicit capability flag rather than a None, and the test-side skip should route through the not-verified tier carrying the remedy command, so the roll-up shows an unanswered question rather than a pass or an unexplained failure. MEASURED, and the measurement is why this is not a program rule: a static screen over the tree gives 131 guarded imports, 79 using an attribute outside the handler, 56 with no capability guard, and 8 once sibling and standard-library imports are excluded — and of the 6 of those 8 that can be executed with the dependency blocked, 6 of 6 degrade with a message and none crashes. The static form does not work. The motivating defect was never the absent case at all: it was an attribute that arrived in the dependency's next major release, on a host that had the older one, costing 33 red test identifiers and one crash returned under the exit code reserved for a design finding. EXISTING PARTIAL COVERAGE, which this record failed to cite and which the implementing lane should build on rather than reinvent: the tests tree already carries a shared helper for exactly the too-old case, used by three test files. Its own header records the measurement -- on a host carrying the 3.2.0 release, 33 of the 46 shipped test files in this layer failed from that single cause, every one of them reporting as a FAILURE rather than as a skip. The helper degrades to the older draft AND pins that the degradation is honest: the schema must use no keyword the two drafts read differently, and every internal reference must be a local pointer, because a bare-name identifier is not a resolvable address and a remote reference would send the validator to a host that does not exist. What is still missing, and why this stays Bucket C, is the matrix: the helper handles the version this machine happens to have, and nothing exercises BOTH versions, so the next incompatibility is found the same way this one was.
session_context: Raised while distilling a measurement layer's end-to-end lane cluster. Began as a Bucket-A static rule and was demoted by its own corpus sweep: four narrowings, all over-reporting, and every executable survivor behaving correctly.

design: one measurement layer of 26 modules; no design involved
rule_name: a contract relation is not an import edge and owes a pair test
pattern: Two modules agree on a document shape: one writes it, the other reads and validates it. Neither imports the other — the writer builds a plain mapping and the reader receives one — so the relation exists in the SHARED VOCABULARY and nowhere in the code. Dependency analysis cannot see it, the module graph shows the two as unrelated, and each side's suite exercises only its own reading of the shape. Both suites pass. The disagreement is reachable only by driving the two together, which nothing does, so the defect ships and is found by whoever first runs the layer end to end.
docstring: Where two modules share a document-shape identifier and neither imports the other, they have a contract with no code relation, and that pair owes a test that exercises BOTH sides — the real producer's output handed to the real consumer. This is the seam class that per-module suites cannot reach by construction, not by oversight: a suite that imports one module is testing one reading of a two-sided agreement, and a second reading it never loads cannot contradict it. Exclude the vocabulary token that most modules carry before counting, or the pair set explodes into every combination and the real seams drown in it.
fix_action: Collect, per module, the document-shape identifiers it names as string literals. Drop any identifier carried by more than two modules — that is the layer's universal record type, not a contract between a pair. Every remaining identifier shared by exactly two modules is a producer/consumer contract: require a test file whose imports include BOTH modules, and report each pair that has none. MEASURED ON THIS LAYER: 6 contract pairs; 0 of 6 have an import edge, so a dependency-graph check finds none of them; 5 of 6 now have a pair test, all added by the lanes that repaired the seam defects; and 1 of 6 has NEITHER — a live seam of exactly the shape that produced four of the eighteen findings. Guard the detector's own denominator: without the generic-token exclusion the same layer reports 47 pairs, and the 6 that matter are indistinguishable from the 41 that do not.

design: any host with an older release of an optional dependency; no design involved
rule_name: optional_import_is_guarded_by_capability_not_exception_type
title: an optional import is guarded by capability not by exception type
pattern: An optional dependency is imported inside a handler that catches the import failure, and the fallback is correct for the case where the package is missing entirely. The package is then used through an attribute that only exists from a later release. On a host carrying an older release the import SUCCEEDS, the handler never runs, and the attribute access raises — inside a program whose exit codes reserve one value for a finding about the subject under test, so a crash publishes itself as a verdict. The test-side guard has the same hole from the other side: skipping on whether the import works covers one of the two ways the dependency can be out of reach.
docstring: Guard an optional dependency on the CAPABILITY the code uses, never on whether the import raised. Present-but-too-old and absent are different states and only one of them is an import failure; the guard that conflates them fails on the state that is harder to notice, because everything up to the attribute access behaves normally. The same rule binds the test side: a skip predicated on importability reports NOT-RUN for the absent case and a red for the too-old one, and neither is the honest answer, which is that the verification did not run and here is the command that would let it.
fix_action: For every handler catching an import failure and binding a name, require a capability check on each attribute of that name used outside the handler, and make the fallback path set an explicit capability flag the use sites read. Route the test-side skip through the not-verified tier rather than a bare skip, carrying the remedy command, so the roll-up sees an unanswered question instead of a green tick. Measured cost of the version-gated case: the gate crashed and returned the exit code reserved for a finding about the subject, and 33 test identifiers were red on a stock host for that one attribute. A broad static screen over this tree finds 79 of 131 handler sites using an attribute of the guarded name outside the handler; that is an UPPER BOUND on candidates and not a defect count, because a site whose use is already behind a capability flag satisfies the rule and the screen cannot see the flag.

design: the plugin's own instruction surface; no design involved
rule_name: a documented command must be accepted by the program it names
pattern: Shipped documentation quotes a command as the way to run a tool. The tool's options change; the document does not, because nothing relates the two. An existing guard may already check that the named FILE exists — which it does — so the command looks verified while the invocation itself has never been tried. An agent following the instruction literally gets an argument error and no output, and the document that sent it there is the same document a reviewer would consult to confirm the instruction is right.
docstring: Every command quoted in shipped instruction text must be ACCEPTED by the program it names, not merely name a file that exists. Two extensions over the usual form of this guard, and each was needed to see a real case: the population must include the instruction surface an agent actually follows, not only the release notes and manifests; and the test must reach the OPTIONS, because a stale flag and a correct one point at the same existing file.
fix_action: Join backslash continuations FIRST, then extract each quoted invocation, then decide acceptance from the program's own declared options — or by invoking it in a way that can only fail on argument parsing. Report the document, the program and the offending options. MEASURED: 165 quoted commands name a program that exists; 11 use an option the program neither declares nor mentions; 2 of those 11 confirmed by running them, one reporting `unrecognized arguments` outright and both exiting on an argument error. WRITE THE SCREEN CAREFULLY — mine was wrong twice, in opposite directions, on this same corpus: matching greedily across lines bled the trailing compliance block into the preceding command and reported 47, and confining the match to one line excluded every multi-line invocation and reported 0, missing the one case already proven by execution. A checker for this that is itself built by grep will reproduce one of those two numbers. INVOCATION SWEEP, AND THE MASKING RULE IT TAUGHT: of the 11 static candidates, 8 are now CONFIRMED by running them and reporting unrecognized arguments; 3 remain masked rather than cleared. ARGPARSE REPORTS ONE ERROR, so a missing required argument is announced first and HIDES an unrecognized flag on the same command line. A naive invocation test therefore clears cases it has not tested: it confirmed 4 of the 11, and supplying the required arguments took that to 8 with no change to the documents. Satisfy required arguments first, or read the parser's declared actions instead of invoking. RE-RUN after merging main and still failing identically -- rc 2, 'the following arguments are required', with the declared form returning 0 as the control. The offending text is located exactly, in the repository and not only in the installed copy: `skills/benchmark-enhancement-capture/SKILL.md` line 532, a four-line continued invocation whose three output flags were all replaced by one. It is deliberately NOT hand-patched here -- the record's claim is that a checker must catch the class, and one corrected line would leave the population unguarded while making the motivating instance disappear.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: a tool-error verdict must carry the tool's own diagnostic
pattern: A step drives an external tool, the tool exits without a usable result, and the step records a verdict meaning tool-error. The verdict text names the tool as the cause. The tool's own message is not retained anywhere. Downstream a gate reads that verdict and repeats the attribution in its own finding — so the claim that the tool failed is asserted twice by two layers, neither of which saw the tool's output. The attribution is then unfalsifiable: a genuine tool defect and a setup gap in the step's own invocation produce a byte-identical record, and the only way to tell them apart is to reproduce the run.
docstring: A verdict that attributes a failure to an external tool must carry that tool's own diagnostic — its exit status and the tail of what it wrote — or it must not name the tool. Without the diagnostic the record cannot be routed to a layer: the same verdict is produced by a defect in the tool and by a missing input the step was supposed to supply, and those two are fixed in different repositories. A consumer of the verdict must not restate the attribution it inherited, because repeating an unevidenced claim at a second layer makes it look corroborated.
fix_action: At the site that INVOKES the tool, capture its exit status and a bounded tail of its output into the artefact beside the verdict, and make the tool-error branch refuse to write a verdict that names a tool without them. At the consuming gate, derive the finding text from the retained diagnostic rather than from a literal, and where none is present say that the failure was not attributed rather than naming a tool. MEASURED, AND IT SETTLED A QUESTION THAT HAD BEEN OPEN ACROSS THIS WHOLE LANE: a post-layout equivalence failure could not be assigned to the tool or to the invocation, because the consuming gate never runs the tool and the producing step retains nothing from it. The tree itself supplies the answer the record could not: the runner's own helper documents this exact abort — physical-only cells present in the routed netlist and absent from the timing library make the tool stop before the comparison starts — and calls it a FALSE tool-error, fixing it by emitting blackbox stubs. So the failure class is the step's own setup, NOT the tool, and the record that would have sent it to the forked-tool repository was never written. CORPUS-SWEPT, AND THE SWEEP MOVED THE CHECK TO THE ARTEFACT. A code scan cannot answer this. The verdict lives in a constant rather than a literal, so a literal scan finds one site of the several that exist; and asking whether the FILE mentions an exit status or an output tail is meaningless when the producing file is tens of thousands of lines long — it says yes for reasons that have nothing to do with this artefact. The predicate is artefact-level: does the written record carry a diagnostic beside a verdict that names a tool? Measured on the one record of this kind in the tree, the keys are verdict, tool, top, skipped and a skip reason — it NAMES the tool and carries nothing from it. AND THERE IS NO SCHEMA FOR THE ARTEFACT, which is why nothing requires the field: the rule's real home is a schema that makes the diagnostic mandatory whenever the verdict names a tool, not a scan over source. THE SHARPEST INSTANCE IS THIS BATCH'S OWN BUCKET-T RECORD, found by checking its samples instead of trusting that the paths resolved. That record cites a signal and an exit code of 139 for ten crashing arms. Every one of the ten committed directories holds three JSON files and nothing else -- no log, no report, no error file -- and each records a runner exit of 1. The GOLDEN arm records 1 as well, so on the only status field the artefacts carry, the crashing arms and the passing one are identical. The tool's actual status and output survived only in a session transcript that was never committed. The consequence is concrete and not stylistic: the record cannot be filed upstream, because a maintainer who receives those directories can reproduce nothing. That is what this rule buys -- not tidier artefacts, but the difference between a fork bug that can be handed over and one that cannot. THE COST IS NOW PERMANENT ON THIS INSTANCE, which is the part a reader should take from it. The diagnostic was not merely unretained at the time; the run trees that held it have since been removed from the host, so the evidence cannot be recovered at all -- only regenerated by re-running the fault. A rule that says 'retain the tool's own output' reads like tidiness until the window closes, and then it reads like the difference between a fork bug that can be filed and one that must be reproduced from scratch first. AND THE OBVIOUS REMEDY IS THE WRONG ONE, which is worth saying before someone builds it. A reader meeting this record naturally reaches for provenance -- declare the artefacts by digest so they can be found later. That is already done, universally: across the cross-layer trial contracts, 525 of 525 evidence artefacts carry a content digest beside their path, role and byte count, and it works -- the published baseline was RECOVERED by hash after its source project ceased to exist on the host, by searching for the declared digests and finding one tree that carried all three byte-identically. So the evidence manifest is not the gap. The gap is that the tool's own exit status and output tail were never made artefacts at all, so there was nothing for a digest to point at. Adding provenance to this record's subject would produce a perfectly-hashed manifest of everything except the thing needed to file the bug.

design: one routed digital core, open PDK; identifier withheld per capture honesty rule
rule_name: an admitted lever must report its applicable site count
pattern: A search space decides, per lever, whether the specification permits turning it, and publishes the admitted set with a count. Permission is a property of the SPECIFICATION; having somewhere to apply it is a property of the DESIGN, and the document conflates them. A lever that is permitted but has no applicable site on this design is admitted, counted, and indistinguishable in the published record from one with many sites — so the space advertises a dimensionality it does not have, a reader plans a sweep against it, and the shortfall only appears when somebody tries to author a candidate and finds there is nothing to change.
docstring: Admission answers whether a lever MAY be turned; it does not answer whether there is anything here to turn. Both belong in the published space, per lever, because a consumer sizing a search reads the admitted count as the number of dimensions available to it. A lever admitted with zero applicable sites is not a search dimension, and a space that cannot say so overstates itself in the one field a planner uses. Report the count rather than dropping the lever: zero sites on this design is a measurement about the design, and silently withholding an admitted lever would hide it.
fix_action: Give each lever an applicable-site counter over the design's own sources — for a state-encoding lever the number of state-holding control structures, for a hierarchy lever the number of module boundaries eligible to move, and so on — and publish the count beside `admitted` on every lever. Report a lever admitted with a count of zero as a distinct, non-fatal finding, and subtract it from the count a planner reads, or publish both totals so the difference is visible. Where a lever's sites cannot be counted deterministically, emit the count as not-measured with the reason rather than as zero: an uncounted lever and an inapplicable one must not look alike, which is the same sentinel rule the record layer already enforces. MEASURED on the published space document: `admitted_count` is 5, every one of the 5 admitted levers carries the same ten keys, and NONE of those keys is a site count — while on that design one of the 5 had no applicable site at all, being a pure datapath with no control state to re-encode. The lane that hit this authored no candidate for it and said so in prose; nothing in the machine-readable space records it. SWEPT, and it finds a false positive the rule would produce on the very document that motivated it. Of the five admitted levers, four are DESIGN-scoped -- an arithmetic architecture applies to arithmetic units, a hierarchy choice to modules, a pipelining offset to output paths, a state encoding to state machines -- and for those an applicable-site count is exactly the right question, and exactly what is missing. The fifth is a synthesis strategy, which is TOOL-scoped: it is handed to the tool once for the whole run, and it has no sites to count. A rule demanding a site count from every admitted lever therefore reports 5 and one of them is wrong -- and it is wrong in the expensive direction, because a planner told that a global setting has an unreported site count learns nothing and distrusts the other four. The discriminator already exists in the published document: every lever carries a `layer`, and the tool-scoped one is the only entry whose layer names a tool stage rather than a level of the design. BUILD: require an applicable-site count from design-scoped levers, and from a tool-scoped lever require the disclosure that fits it -- that it applies once, to the run -- so the space says which of its dimensions can move on THIS design and which are settings. A SECOND CLAUSE, stated explicitly because it is a different question the same document owes the same reader, and folding it into a sentence is how two gaps in this batch became invisible. The first clause asks whether a lever CAN move on this design. The second asks whether it DID. The published space answers neither: it reports five admitted levers and an empty self-audit, and the source that produced it says in prose that three of the five were admitted and never searched -- deliberately, with reasons. Probed for a field that would carry that distinction (searched, turned, exercised, skipped, unused, not-searched): none is present. The document does carry a list of place-and-route levers excluded on purpose, so the shape of such a disclosure already exists one field over and simply was not extended to the admitted set. The consequence for a consumer is arithmetic: it reads coverage of five where the run turned two, and nothing in the machine-readable space contradicts it. So the rule is that an admitted lever discloses BOTH its applicable site count and whether this run exercised it, and one check over the space document enforces both because the population and the owner are the same.

design: two published record trees of one measurement layer; open PDK
rule_name: a provenance path convention must be declared and identical across producers
pattern: A record type carries a provenance field naming the artefact it was read from. Each producer fills it with whatever its own reader happened to hold — one resolves to an absolute path, another keeps the path relative to the project root — and the record schema never says which is meant. The split is per PRODUCER, so it is invisible from inside any one of them and perfectly consistent within each. Downstream, anything that compares, de-duplicates or cites by that field sees two conventions for one fact; and the absolute half carries the filesystem prefix of whichever machine ran it, so the published record is machine-specific in a field a reader trusts as neutral.
docstring: The convention of a provenance field is part of the record contract and must be stated once and enforced for every producer, not left to whatever each reader happens to hold. Two conventions for one field is a disagreement even when each side is internally perfect, because the consumer cannot tell which it has without knowing who wrote it. And a provenance path must be expressed relative to a declared root: an absolute one embeds the machine, which makes a published record unreproducible and leaks a filesystem layout into an artefact meant to describe a measurement.
fix_action: State the convention in the record definition — a path relative to the declared run root — and enforce it where the record is CONSTRUCTED, so no producer can supply the other form. Refuse a path that resolves outside the declared root, and refuse an absolute one outright rather than rewriting it: rewriting invents provenance, and a path that is not the path that was read is not provenance. Where a producer genuinely cannot express its artefact relative to the root, it must record the root it used beside the path rather than silently switching form. MEASURED across the two published record trees: 6867 records carry an absolute path and 6674 a relative one, and the split is perfectly per producer — three producers always relative, two always absolute. EVERY ONE of the 6867 absolute paths embeds a host home directory. The existing portability guard cannot see any of this: it walks emitted scripts by file suffix and never opens a record. CORRECTED BY RE-MEASUREMENT, and the correction makes the rule MORE necessary rather than less. The original narrative said the split was perfectly per producer, each producer flawlessly self-consistent, so the disagreement was invisible from inside any one of them. Re-run independently over both record trees, grouping on `source.tool` (the field that actually names the producing tool) and again on the metric family, the split is NOT clean under either: two tools are mixed and three metric families are mixed. So the convention is inconsistent WITHIN producers, not merely between them -- which removes the excuse that no single author could have seen it, and means a per-producer fix would not converge. What DOES reproduce, and is the part with a consequence, is the host prefix: of the absolute paths, every single one begins with a home directory, 6804 of 6804, against 5330 relative paths that carry no host at all. The predicate must therefore be stated over the field and not over the producer -- every `source.path` in a published record resolves the same way, declared once -- and the check must run per record, because grouping by producer is what hid the inconsistency in the first place. SWEPT, and the sweep removes the objection that has been blocking this fix. The source lane declined to rewrite the paths, reasoning that a recorded path which is not the path that was read is not provenance -- which is right, and would forbid the repair if any producer were reading files it could not express relatively. Measured: all 6804 absolute paths sit under exactly TWO roots, and both are the producing run's own directory. NOT ONE points outside a run tree. So there is no case where absolute is forced, every one of them is expressible against its run root, and a run-root-relative path IS still the path that was read -- merely stated against a declared base instead of against the machine. The false-positive population for a check demanding the declared convention is therefore zero on this corpus, and the objection that kept 6804 host home directories in a field readers treat as neutral does not apply. BUILD: declare the base in the record beside the path, require every producer to state its paths against it, and the check becomes a prefix test rather than a rewrite.

design: thirteen rewrite candidates over one routed digital core, open PDK
rule_name: a cheap fidelity rung may not rank candidates until its rank agreement is measured
pattern: A search offers an ordered fidelity ladder, cheapest first, so candidates can be screened early and only survivors carried to the expensive rung. The cheap rung measures a quantity that CORRELATES with the signed-off one but does not order the candidates the same way, because the expensive stage charges for something the cheap one cannot see. Screening then discards the true winner before it is ever measured, and the run looks efficient: every surviving candidate was evaluated properly, the budget was respected, and the one that would have won is simply absent from the results with no trace that it was dropped.
